newsitem.title: CANADA: Re-elected Canada government to keep deficit focus.
newsitem.headline: Re-elected Canada government to keep deficit focus.

text.p: Canada's recently re-elected Liberal government made clear on Thursday that it would keep up its fight against the country's budget deficit and resist pressure to increase spending.
"We will maintain our course of having no deficit within two years," Prime Minister Jean Chretien told reporters after the first cabinet retreat since his government was re-elected on June 2.
"This government is not veering left or right," he said. "It's moving forward. Sometimes you have curves to the left, sometimes curves to the right, but you're always moving forward."
The Liberals squeaked through with a second majority government last week, winning 155 of 301 parliamentary seats. The party lost two-thirds of its seats in economically depressed Atlantic Canada.

The slim majority means the Liberals must pay more attention to their left-leaning legislators, who are pushing for a return to the party's roots -- more spending on social programs and a reduced emphasis on deficit reduction.

The Liberal government's proudest achievement in its first term was slashing the deficit from a once huge C$42 billion ($30.3 billion) in 1993 to an estimated C$15 billion ($10.8 billion) now. The final numbers for fiscal 1996-97 will not be released until the autumn.
"The pressure on us is to stay the course and make sure that interest rates stay down and jobs are created," Finance Minister Paul Martin said after the cabinet meeting.
Despite strong economic fundamentals in Canada and more than a year of low interest rates, unemployment is stubbornly high, hovering just below 10 percent.
Chretien said the government was concerned about child poverty and the lack of jobs for young people.
But the struggle within the cabinet centered on how quickly the government should move on those problems.
The Liberals have already moved to loosen the purse strings, promising in the election campaign to cancel scheduled funding cuts to health care.
They have also pledged to double an C$850 million ($614 million) tax credit for families with children, but have not committed to a timetable.
"Our electoral commitment is to increase that payment to fight child poverty the minute that our deficit is eliminated," Human Resources Development Minister Pierre Pettigrew said.
But Industry Minister John Manley, considered to be on the right wing of the Liberal party, emphasized the need to tackle the debt once the deficit was licked.
"We've fundamentally staked...our hope for the future and securing our future on the basis that we are going to manage the public finances in a responsible way," Manley told reporters.
"That requires that we continue on the course of deficit elimination and we will require over time that we deal with the issue of the level of our debt."
Canada's debt is expected to total C$610.3 billion ($441 billion) in 1997-98, or about 73.1 percent of gross domestic product.
